content:
If arthritis and frailty make it hard to get around your home, adaptations such as a stairlift, a level-access shower or a ramp can help you stay safe and independent. A Disabled Facilities Grant (DFG) from your council can help with the cost.

This guide explains who can apply, how much is available, and how the process usually works. Check the details with your own council, as processes vary.

What a DFG can pay for

  • Stairlifts and through-floor lifts.
  • Level-access showers and wet rooms.
  • Ramps and widened doorways.
  • Changes to heating or lighting controls to make them easier to use.
  • Other changes that help you get in and around your home.

How much you can get

According to GOV.UK, you can apply for up to:

  • £30,000 in England.
  • £36,000 in Wales.
  • £25,000 in Northern Ireland.

Some councils may give more. How much you get usually depends on household income and savings over £6,000, so you may need to pay towards the cost. Disabled Facilities Grants are not available in Scotland, where councils offer other support for equipment and adaptations.

Who can apply

You or someone living in the property must be disabled, and you must intend to live there for the grant period. Owners and tenants can apply, and landlords can apply for tenants.

How the process usually works

  • Contact your council (in Northern Ireland, the Housing Executive or your Health and Social Care Trust).
  • An occupational therapist usually assesses your needs and recommends the adaptations.
  • The council checks the work is necessary, appropriate, reasonable and practical, and may carry out a means test.
  • Get quotes and wait for approval. Do not start work before the council approves your application, or you may not get a grant.

Smaller adaptations and equipment

In England, minor adaptations costing under £1,000, such as grab rails, and equipment like perching stools, are usually provided free after a care needs assessment. Ask your council or occupational therapist.

Delays

Waiting times can be long. Ask about interim equipment while you wait, and tell the council if your needs change.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Will I have to pay back the grant?

Usually not, but some councils can ask for repayment if you sell the property within a set time after work over a certain value.

Can I choose my own builder?

Often yes, as long as the council agrees. Some councils use their own approved contractors.

Does it cover moving home?

Some councils offer help with moving if adapting is not practical. Ask your council.
